title: Declaring Variables with let, const, and var
ques: Explain the differences between **`var`**, **`let`**, and **`const`** in modern JavaScript regarding re-assignment, block scope, and hoisting.
explanation: `const` is preferred by default for values that never reassign. `let` is used for accumulators and loops. `var` is avoided in modern JS due to lack of block scoping and hoisting bugs.

title: JavaScript Primitive and Reference Data Types
ques: List the seven primitive data types in JavaScript along with reference types. Write a snippet demonstrating the `typeof` operator on each.

answer.content:
// Primitives (stored by value)
const aString = "Hello";              // string
const aNumber = 42;                   // number
const aBigInt = 9007199254740991n;    // bigint
const aBoolean = true;                // boolean
const anUndefined = undefined;        // undefined
const aSymbol = Symbol("id");         // symbol
const aNull = null;                   // null (typeof evaluates to 'object' due to historical JS bug)

// Reference Types (stored by memory reference pointer)
const anObject = { name: "Alice" };   // object
const anArray = [1, 2, 3];            // object (Array.isArray(anArray) is true)
const aFunction = function() {};      // function

console.log(typeof aString);    // 'string'
console.log(typeof aNumber);    // 'number'
console.log(typeof aNull);      // 'object' (legacy quirk)
console.log(typeof aFunction);  // 'function'

explanation: JavaScript has 7 primitives: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `null`. Objects, arrays, and functions are reference types.

title: Working with Operators in JavaScript
ques: Contrast strict equality (`===`) with loose equality (`==`), and demonstrate arithmetic, logical, and ternary operators.
explanation: Always prefer `===` and `!==` to prevent unintended implicit type coercion. Logical operators (`||`, `&&`, `??`) allow concise fallback evaluations.

title: JavaScript Syntax Fundamentals and Statements
ques: Explain the rules of JavaScript syntax regarding case sensitivity, semicolons, comments, and identifiers. Write a properly formatted script calculating circle properties.
explanation: JavaScript identifiers use camelCase conventions and are case-sensitive. Exponentiation is written using `**`, and comments use `//` or `/* */`.
